findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build downloads and executes whatever the remote URL serves as root in the build container. The script has no pinned version or integrity check, so a compromised endpoint or changed response can execute arbitrary code and alter the resulting image.

findings.title: Fail the build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline returns the status of sh, not curl. If curl cannot connect and produces no output, sh successfully executes an empty input, so Docker reports a successful installation step even though the installer never ran. The -s option also suppresses curl's error message.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it

findings.title: Fail the build when the installer cannot be downloaded
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline reports the exit status of sh, so a curl connection failure that produces no output can leave sh exiting successfully. Docker then continues building an image even though the install step did not run. The -s option also hides the download error.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every uncached build executes whatever the remote URL returns as root in the image build. The URL is neither version-pinned nor verified, so a compromised or changed response can inject code into the image or access build-time resources.

findings.title: Fail the build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline returns the exit status of sh, not curl. They now fail TypeScript compilation; existing JavaScript callers encounter a rejected promise when a positive-stock reservation accesses the missing store, and callers using the returned promise as a boolean treat even an unavailable item as successfully reserved.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: With one unit loaded, two concurrent calls both read remaining=1 before either save finishes. Both save 0 and return true, so two customers receive a successful reservation for one unit.

findings.title: Preserve or explicitly migrate the exported reservation API
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve previously returned a boolean synchronously and now returns a Promise. Existing TypeScript callers expecting boolean no longer compile, while JavaScript callers using if (inventory.reserve(sku)) treat even a reservation that resolves to false as truthy. Existing callers also construct Inventory without a Store, which now causes reserve to fail when stock is available.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: The await occurs before the in-memory stock is decremented. With one unit loaded, two concurrent calls can both read 1, both save 0, and both return true, granting two reservations for one unit. Previously, the synchronous decrement occurred before another call could read the stock.

findings.title: Preserve the synchronous reservation contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported reserve method now returns a Promise instead of a boolean. Existing TypeScript callers expecting a boolean fail to compile; JavaScript callers such as `if (inventory.reserve(sku))` treat even an out-of-stock result as truthy and proceed.

findings.title: Keep existing inventory construction working
findings.whyItBreaks: Inventory previously had a public zero-argument constructor. Existing TypeScript consumers using `new Inventory()` now fail to compile, while JavaScript consumers can still construct it but fail when reserving available stock because `this.store` is undefined.

findings.title: Update the retry caller for millisecond backoff values
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry still multiplies it by 1,000 before sleeping. The first retry therefore waits 1,000 seconds instead of one second, and later delays reach 30,000 seconds instead of 30 seconds. The final failed attempt also incurs this delay before the error is thrown.

findings.title: Update the retry caller for millisecond backoff values
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry still multiplies that value by 1,000 before passing it to sleep. The first retry therefore waits 1,000 seconds instead of one second; the capped delay grows from 30 seconds to 30,000 seconds.

findings.title: Update the retry caller for millisecond backoff values
findings.whyItBreaks: The retry caller still multiplies backoff by 1,000 before passing it to a millisecond timer. After the first failure, it now sleeps for 1,000 seconds instead of 1 second; at the cap it sleeps for 30,000 seconds instead of 30 seconds. It also sleeps after the final failed attempt, delaying delivery of the error.

findings.title: Propagate file close errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred Close discards its error. If Flush succeeds but the filesystem reports a delayed write error on Close, Save returns nil, so callers cannot distinguish a failed save from a successful one. Previously, the successful-flush path returned the Close error.

findings.title: Propagate errors from closing the saved file
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred Close return value is discarded. If Flush succeeds but Close reports a delayed filesystem write error, Save now returns nil, so callers cannot distinguish a failed save from a successful one. Previously, Save returned the Close error.

findings.title: Propagate the output file's close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred Close discards its error. If Flush succeeds but Close reports a delayed write or filesystem error, the public Save function returns nil even though the save failed. Previously, Save returned the Close error to its caller.

findings.title: Include the final row in each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: Python's range excludes its upper bound, so subtracting one from the already exclusive end drops the last row of every nonempty page. For example, page_window(['a', 'b'], 0, 2) returns only ['a']; pages of size one return no rows. render_page and summarize inherit the loss.

findings.title: Preserve the existing public keyword parameters
findings.whyItBreaks: Renaming page and size to page_index and page_size makes existing calls such as page_window(rows, page=0, size=10) raise TypeError. The same compatibility break affects keyword parameters of clamp, page_count, render_page, and summarize.

findings.title: Include the final row in each page
findings.whyItBreaks: The end bound is already exclusive, so subtracting one drops the last row of every nonempty page. For example, page_window(['a', 'b'], 0, 2) returns only ['a']; pages of size one are always empty. render_page and summarize therefore silently omit rows.

findings.title: Preserve the public keyword argument names
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing Python callers can pass arguments by keyword. Renaming page and size to page_index and page_size makes calls such as page_window(rows, page=0, size=10) raise TypeError. The same incompatible rename affects clamp, page_count, render_page, and summarize.

findings.title: Include the final row in each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: The end bound is already exclusive, so subtracting one omits the last row of every nonempty page. For example, page_window(['a', 'b'], 0, 2) returns only ['a']; a page containing one row returns an empty list. Both render_page and summarize consequently omit rows from their output.

findings.title: Preserve the existing public keyword parameters
findings.whyItBreaks: Renaming page and size to page_index and page_size makes previously valid calls such as page_window(rows, page=0, size=10) raise TypeError. The same incompatible keyword renaming affects clamp, page_count, render_page, and summarize.

findings.title: Return cached values before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A freshly stored entry has an age below ttlMs, so get deletes it and returns null. If an entry is first read after its TTL, get instead returns the expired value.

findings.title: Remove every completed job when pruning
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing shifts the next job into the current index, but forEach advances to the next index. For two adjacent completed jobs, the second remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's job array
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous public function returned a new array without changing its input. The new implementation removes elements from the caller's array and returns the same reference, so callers retaining the original queue unexpectedly lose completed jobs.

findings.title: Restore the cache expiration comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry is deleted and reported as missing while its age is within the TTL. Conversely, an entry first read after its TTL has elapsed is returned, including at arbitrarily old ages.

findings.title: Remove every completed job
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forEach shifts the next job into the current index, which forEach then skips. For two adjacent completed jobs, the second remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Preserve the input queue when pruning
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation returned a new array and left the caller's array intact. Splicing the supplied array now removes jobs from every other reference to that queue, causing callers that retain the original list to lose those entries.

findings.title: Restore the cache expiration comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: A freshly stored entry has an age below its TTL, so get deletes it and returns null. An entry first read after its TTL instead returns its stale value and remains cached.

findings.title: Remove every completed job
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forEach shifts the next job into the current index, which forEach then skips. For two adjacent completed jobs, the second remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's input queue
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation returned a new array without changing jobs. The new implementation removes elements from the caller's array and returns that same array, so other references to the original queue unexpectedly lose jobs.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, total and rows.length are both zero, so the function now returns NaN instead of the previous result, 0. Callers using the result in arithmetic or serialization receive an invalid value for a previously supported input.

findings.title: Avoid sorting the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates rows, so calling busiest now reorders the caller's data by amount. Previously the function sorted a copy, preserving the original order. A caller that uses the same array afterward will observe changed ordering.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, total and rows.length are both 0, so the exported function returns NaN instead of its previous result of 0. Callers using the result in arithmetic or serialization receive an invalid numeric result.

findings.title: Avoid sorting the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates rows. Calling busiest now reorders the caller's data by amount, whereas the previous implementation sorted a copy. A caller that continues using the original order will observe changed data.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, total and rows.length are both zero, so this returns NaN instead of the previous 0. Callers using the result in arithmetic or serialized output receive a different, invalid numeric result.

findings.title: Avoid sorting the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates rows. Calling busiest with rows ordered by amounts [1, 2] now changes that shared array to [2, 1], whereas the previous implementation left it unchanged. Callers that reuse the original ordering receive reordered data.

findings.title: Restore numeric score sorting
findings.whyItBreaks: The default Array.sort() compares scores as strings. For players with scores 2 and 10, in that order, and n=1, the reversed scores are [2, 10], so the cutoff is 2 and topPlayers returns the player with score 2. formatBoard displays that player as the leader.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before selecting the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator sorts numbers as strings. For players ordered with scores 9 and 100 and n=1, rankScores returns [9, 100], so the cutoff is 9 and topPlayers returns the player with 9 instead of the player with 100. formatBoard displays that incorrect result.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before selecting the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For players with scores 9 and 10, in that order, and n=1, the resulting cutoff is 9, so topPlayers returns the 9-point player instead of the 10-point player. formatBoard consequently displays the wrong winner.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: String equality can take different amounts of time depending on the matching prefix. An attacker able to submit and time repeated webhook requests may use that signal to recover a valid signature and pass the authentication check.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: String equality can take different amounts of time depending on how much of the supplied signature matches. An attacker able to make repeated webhook requests and measure response times may use that timing information to recover a valid signature and cause handle() to invoke the processor for an unauthenticated payload.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: String equality can return after the first differing character, making verification time depend on how much of the supplied signature matches. An attacker able to make repeated webhook requests and measure sufficiently precise timings can use that signal to forge a signature and reach the payload processor.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits after the ledger insert, before either balance update. If a balance update fails or the process stops, the ledger can record a transfer that did not complete. A failure after the debit can also leave the accounts inconsistent, depending on the database connection's transaction behavior. Previously, all three writes were inside the same transaction.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger transaction commits before either balance update runs. If a balance update fails, the ledger entry remains committed; if the credit fails after the debit succeeds, the accounts can also be left inconsistent. Previously all three writes were in the same transaction and rolled back together on failure.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits after inserting the ledger entry, before either balance update runs. If a balance update fails, the ledger entry has already committed; if the destination update fails after the source update, the source may also remain debited. The database can therefore record an incomplete transfer and leave account balances inconsistent.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when calculating the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: The local-time getters change the result for timestamps near midnight UTC on hosts outside UTC. For example, in America/Los_Angeles, 2025-01-01T00:30:00Z now yields 2024-12-31 instead of 2025-01-01. Consequently, sameBillingDay can also classify two timestamps differently depending on the host timezone.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when calculating billing days
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation used UTC date components. The new local-time getters return a different billing day near midnight on hosts outside UTC. For example, 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z becomes 2023-12-31 in America/Los_Angeles. This also changes sameBillingDay comparisons and makes results depend on the server's time zone.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when calculating billing days
findings.whyItBreaks: The local-time getters change the result for dates near midnight whenever the host is not on UTC. For example, with TZ=America/Los_Angeles, 2025-01-01T00:30:00Z now produces 2024-12-31 instead of 2025-01-01. Consequently, sameBillingDay can classify two timestamps on the same UTC day as different billing days, and results can differ between hosts.

findings.title: Include the tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After readProfile('tenant-a', 'alice', fetchProfile) caches a profile, readProfile('tenant-b', 'alice', fetchProfile) uses the same key and returns tenant-a's profile without calling fetchProfile. This exposes profile data across tenants and returns the wrong result.

findings.title: Include the tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After readProfile('tenant-a', 'alice', ...) caches a profile, readProfile('tenant-b', 'alice', ...) hits the same key and returns tenant-a's profile without calling the supplied fetcher. This exposes one tenant's profile to another and returns incorrect data.

findings.title: Include the tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The cache is shared across calls but is now keyed only by account. After readProfile('tenant-a', 'alice', fetchProfile) caches a profile, readProfile('tenant-b', 'alice', fetchProfile) returns tenant-a's profile without calling the fetcher. This exposes profile data across tenants and returns incorrect results.

findings.title: Propagate failures from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw an error, but now returns the same empty string as a key whose stored value is "". Other errors thrown by store.get are also swallowed. The exported load API cannot distinguish failure from a legitimate value, and loadAll now returns an array containing empty strings where it previously threw.

findings.title: Propagate store lookup failures
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw an error, but now returns the same empty string as a key whose stored value is empty. The catch also suppresses errors thrown by store.get. Callers of the exported load API cannot distinguish either failure from a successful lookup; loadAll likewise returns an empty string in its results instead of propagating the error.

findings.title: Propagate lookup failures to callers
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw an error; it now returns the same empty string as a successfully stored empty value. The catch also hides errors thrown by store.get. Consequently, loadAll returns an array containing an empty string instead of failing when a lookup fails, so callers cannot distinguish incomplete data from valid data.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility with existing retry configurations
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers supplying { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer satisfy Config. Existing JavaScript callers continue to run, but config.timeout is undefined, making the deadline NaN; the deadline comparison is then always false, so their configured timeout is silently disabled.

findings.title: Run background retries asynchronously
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported retryBackground function invokes fn synchronously and completes every attempt before returning. A caller relying on background execution instead blocks for the full duration of the attempts, and synchronous side effects happen before the call returns.

findings.title: Expose exhausted retry failures to callers
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function catches every callback exception and returns void after the final attempt, exactly as it does when the callback succeeds. Callers cannot detect that all attempts failed and may treat an operation that never completed as successful.

findings.title: Preserve the existing retry configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing callers pass { maxAttempts, timeoutMs }. They no longer type-check because timeoutMs was removed and retries and timeout are required. JavaScript callers using the old object also compute a NaN deadline, so the timeout never stops retries.

findings.title: Make background retries actually run in the background
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground invokes fn directly before returning and can run every attempt synchronously. A caller using the public name's background behavior to avoid blocking instead blocks until fn and its retries finish.

findings.title: Run the initial attempt when retries is zero
findings.whyItBreaks: The public retries field denotes retries after an initial attempt, but the loop uses it as the total attempt count. With retries: 0, fn is never called; with retries: 1, it is called only once and is never retried.

findings.title: Expose failure after background retries are exhausted
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public function catches every callback error and returns void after exhaustion, exactly as it does after success. Callers cannot distinguish a completed operation from one that failed on every attempt or report the failure.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility with the existing retry configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers passing { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer compile because Config now requires retries and timeout. Existing JavaScript callers still pass timeoutMs, so config.timeout is undefined and the deadline becomes NaN; the deadline comparison then always fails and the timeout is silently disabled.

findings.title: Run background retries outside the caller's synchronous execution
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported retryBackground name promises background execution, but it invokes fn synchronously and runs every attempt before returning. A slow callback therefore blocks the caller, and callers cannot proceed while retries run.

findings.title: Expose failure when background retries are exhausted
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from fn is discarded, and exhaustion returns the same void value as success. The new public API gives callers no way to distinguish a completed operation from one that failed on every attempt, so they can report or act on a failed operation as if it succeeded.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now permits numbers, but TypeScript rejects value.length because number has no length property. The component therefore fails type-checking; if emitted without type-checking, a numeric value produces the label "len=undefined".

findings.title: Preserve the supplied value as the input default
findings.whyItBreaks: A caller supplying value="hello" previously got an input initialized to "hello"; it now gets "len=5". Users see and submit the label instead of the supplied field value.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before accessing length
findings.whyItBreaks: The declared type is string | number, but number has no length property, so TypeScript reports an error on value.length. If the code is transpiled without type-checking, a numeric value such as 42 produces the label len=undefined.

findings.title: Preserve the supplied input value
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing string values are replaced by their lengths: value="hello" now initializes the input to "len=5" instead of "hello". Users viewing or submitting the field receive different data from what the caller supplied.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now permits numbers, but number has no length property. TypeScript reports TS2339, preventing a normal type-checked build. If transpiled without type checking, a numeric value produces the label "len=undefined".

findings.title: Preserve the supplied input value
findings.whyItBreaks: The input previously initialized with the supplied value. It now initializes with a length label instead: value="hello" displays and submits "len=5" rather than "hello", so forms using this component can submit incorrect data.

findings.title: Restore the Git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer reduces spawnSync's output limit from 64 MiB to Node's 1 MiB default. A PR whose git diff exceeds 1 MiB now causes git() to throw before review starts. That call also occurs before the try block, so runGithub cannot post its failure check.

findings.title: Restore the Git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer lowers Node's spawnSync output limit from 64 MiB to its 1 MiB default. A PR whose git diff exceeds 1 MiB now fails while constructing the patch, before review() runs. Because this happens before the try block, the adapter also cannot post its intended failure check. Such diffs previously fit within the configured limit.

findings.title: Restore the Git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer reduces spawnSync's output limit from 64 MiB to Node's default 1 MiB. A pull request whose diff exceeds 1 MiB causes the git diff call at line 140 to fail before review starts. That call is outside the review try/catch, so the adapter also cannot post its intended failure check.

findings.title: Preserve the read-only sandbox for Codex invocations
findings.whyItBreaks: Without the explicit read-only sandbox, Codex can use a more permissive sandbox configured in the invoking environment. A review prompt or instructions in the reviewed repository can then cause the agent to modify files or execute commands with write access to the workspace, whereas this invocation previously forced read-only access.

findings.title: Keep the explicit read-only sandbox for Codex
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous command forced read-only execution. Without that option, Codex can inherit a writable sandbox mode from its configuration. When run against repository content containing malicious instructions, the agent can then modify files in the repository it is reviewing. The prompt alone does not enforce the former sandbox restriction.

findings.title: Keep the read-only sandbox for Codex execution
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit sandbox override allows Codex's effective sandbox mode to come from its configuration. If that configuration permits workspace writes or unrestricted execution, a prompt or repository content can cause the subprocess to modify files or run commands with greater access than this wrapper previously allowed.

findings.title: Compare from the merge base when the target branch has advanced
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current target-branch tip and the PR branch diverged before that tip, diffing directly from PR_BASE_SHA includes the reverse of target-only changes. It can also omit a PR change when both branches independently produce the same result. The review and changed-file list therefore no longer represent the PR's changes, and the resulting verdict can miss or misattribute changes.

findings.title: Generate the patch from the commit being reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checked-out HEAD, such as when Actions checks out a synthetic merge commit, the patch is generated from HEAD while the bundle, review commit_id, and check run identify PR_HEAD_SHA. The adapter can consequently report a successful review for a commit whose actual changes were not reviewed.

findings.title: Diff from the merge base when the target branch has advanced
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA names the current target-branch tip and that branch has advanced since the PR diverged, a two-dot diff from baseSha to HEAD includes reversals of target-only changes. It can also omit a PR change that independently landed on the target branch. The reviewer consequently receives a patch and changed-file list that do not represent the PR, leading to incorrect or missed findings.

findings.title: Generate the patch from the commit being reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checked-out HEAD, the patch now describes HEAD while the bundle, review submission, and check run identify PR_HEAD_SHA. For example, an Actions checkout of a synthetic merge commit can cause the agent to review merged contents and report a passing check on the PR head even though that exact commit was not reviewed.

findings.title: Diff from the merge base when the PR base has advanced
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA names a base-branch commit newer than the branch point, a two-commit diff from that SHA to HEAD includes reversals of base-only changes and can omit PR changes that the base branch independently acquired. The reviewer therefore receives a different patch and changed-file set from the pull request's merge-base diff, potentially missing defects or reporting unrelated changes.

findings.title: Generate the patch from the commit being reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The adapter accepts PR_HEAD_SHA independently of the checked-out HEAD and publishes the review and check against that SHA, but the new patch always ends at HEAD. If the checkout is a synthetic pull-request merge commit or a different revision, the reviewer assesses different contents from the commit receiving the result; a passing check can consequently be attached to unreviewed changes. The previous patch used headSha as its endpoint.

findings.title: Preserve literal replacement text in review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets special sequences in a string replacement. For example, if the serialized bundle contains `$&` in a patch, it is replaced by `{{BUNDLE}}` before the reviewer sees it; `$$`, `$`` and `$'` are also interpreted. The same regression affects the candidate findings and patch replacements on lines 32–33. Patches and findings can legitimately contain these sequences, so both review stages can receive altered evidence and produce incorrect verdicts.

findings.title: Preserve literal replacement tokens in review inputs
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets tokens in a string replacement: for example, a patch containing the literal `$&` is inserted as `{{BUNDLE}}` instead, and `$$` becomes `$`. The same regression affects candidate findings and the critic's patch at lines 32–33. Consequently, both review stages can receive code or findings different from the actual input, leading to missed or incorrect findings.

findings.title: Preserve replacement text literally when assembling prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets special dollar sequences in a string replacement. For example, a patch containing `$$` reaches the reviewer with only one `$`, and `$&` becomes `{{BUNDLE}}`. The same regression affects candidate findings and the critic's patch at lines 32–33. Reviews can therefore analyze different code or findings from those supplied, producing incorrect verdicts.

findings.title: Keep the reviewed commit in the fallback request
findings.whyItBreaks: If the initial request fails and the PR head has advanced while the review was running, omitting commit_id makes GitHub associate the fallback review with the latest PR commit. The review body and verdict were computed from the earlier headSha, while the check is still posted to that earlier SHA. A request for changes can therefore appear against a revision whose code was not reviewed.

findings.title: Keep the reviewed commit on fallback reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: If the initial review request fails and the PR head has advanced since the run captured headSha, the fallback omits commit_id. GitHub then associates the review with the current PR head, although its findings and verdict were computed from the older headSha. This can present a stale review or request for changes as applying to code that was never reviewed.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review bound to the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: If the first review submission fails and a new commit is pushed before the fallback runs, omitting commit_id makes GitHub attach the fallback review to the latest PR commit. The review body and verdict were generated from headSha, so the newer commit receives a review of different code. The check run is still attached to the original headSha.

findings.title: Preserve validation errors for malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizer now converts invalid or missing severity, category, file, line numbers, and required text into ordinary Finding values. For example, normalizeFinding({}) returns a P1 bug with an empty file and line 0; previously it threw. normalizeReview therefore returns an apparently successful review containing an unlocatable, unexplained finding instead of signaling that the review output is malformed. Invalid numeric lines can also become NaN or remain negative.

findings.title: Trim categories before classification
findings.whyItBreaks: A finding with category " security " was previously trimmed and returned as category "security". The new membership check uses the untrimmed value and silently changes its category to "bug", losing the security classification for otherwise accepted input.

findings.title: Retain non-strict review normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizeReview function previously accepted a second strict argument. TypeScript callers passing false now fail to compile, and JavaScript callers passing false no longer get malformed findings filtered out. For example, a findings array containing null previously produced an empty findings array in non-strict mode; it now throws when normalizeFinding reads null.severity.

findings.title: Preserve validation errors for malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: An incomplete finding such as {} previously raised a malformed-finding error in the default review path. It now becomes a P1 bug with an empty file, line 0, and empty explanation and fix. Invalid severity and category values are also silently relabeled, while non-finite or negative line numbers are accepted. Consumers cannot distinguish malformed reviewer output from a real finding and may report the wrong severity or an unusable location.

findings.title: Retain the non-strict normalization option
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function previously accepted normalizeReview(raw, false) to discard malformed findings while retaining the rest of the review. Removing the parameter breaks TypeScript callers at compile time. JavaScript callers still passing false no longer get that behavior: for example, a null finding now throws when normalizeFinding reads raw.severity, aborting the entire review.

findings.title: Restore validation errors for malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid or missing severity and category now become P1 and bug, while missing file and line numbers become an empty path and zero. Previously these inputs threw validation errors. For example, normalizeFinding({}) now returns a seemingly valid Finding that cannot identify a review location, and an unrecognized severity is silently reported as P1. The exported API gives callers no way to distinguish these malformed inputs from legitimate normalized findings.

findings.title: Preserve the lenient normalizeReview parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function previously accepted normalizeReview(raw, false) to discard malformed findings. Removing the second parameter breaks existing TypeScript callers at compile time. JavaScript callers that continue passing false also lose the behavior: a null finding now reaches normalizeFinding and throws instead of being filtered out.

findings.title: Restore the repository argument when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, the event head is empty, so both gh commands run before actions/checkout. On a clean runner workspace there is no Git repository from which gh can infer the target repository, so both commands fail. The surrounding echo commands still succeed and write empty outputs; checkout then falls back to its default ref instead of the PR head, and the review receives empty PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA. On a self-hosted runner with a stale checkout, gh can instead resolve the PR number against the wrong repository.

findings.title: Restore the explicit repository for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: The manual workflow resolves refs before actions/checkout, so gh has no guaranteed Git repository from which to infer the target repository. On a clean runner both lookups fail; on a self-hosted runner with a leftover checkout they can query the wrong repository. The enclosing echo commands still succeed when gh fails, leaving empty ref outputs and allowing checkout to proceed without the requested PR head.

findings.title: Specify the repository when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so both commands run before actions/checkout. Without -R, gh must infer the repository from the runner's current directory. A clean workspace has no Git repository, causing ref resolution to fail; a persistent self-hosted workspace may instead contain a stale checkout and resolve the same PR number against the wrong repository. Because the commands are inside echo substitutions, their failures can also leave empty outputs while the step succeeds.

findings.title: Preserve errors for malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview is exported, but it now converts a missing or non-array findings field to an empty array and similarly defaults malformed residual_risks, checked, and summary fields. For example, null and an otherwise empty review both produce a review with no findings or blocking risks. Previously malformed output threw an error, so callers could reject it; now they cannot distinguish a failed or incomplete review from a valid one and may treat it as clean.

findings.title: Preserve validation errors for malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizeReview function previously threw when required fields were missing or had the wrong type. It now turns invalid findings and residual_risks into empty arrays, and also defaults or coerces invalid summary and checked values. For example, an object with a malformed findings field is returned as a review with no findings, indistinguishable from a valid empty findings list. Callers can no longer detect the malformed output or recover the omitted review information.

findings.title: Reject malformed review output before applying defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizer previously threw when the review was not an object or any required field had the wrong type. It now converts malformed input, including null or a non-array findings field, into a review with empty findings and potentially empty residual risks. Callers cannot distinguish that failure from a legitimate review with no findings or blocking risks.

findings.title: Check out the requested PR head for manual reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event has no pull_request.head.sha, so checkout uses github.ref, the branch selected when starting the workflow, regardless of the required pr_number. The workflow then installs and runs that branch's tool instead of the requested PR's code. Previously it resolved and checked out the requested PR's head SHA.

findings.title: Resolve the requested PR base branch for manual reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event has no pull_request.base.ref, so this always fetches main. If the repository has no main branch, the fetch fails and the review never starts. For a PR targeting another branch, it fetches the wrong base branch instead of the PR's actual base.

findings.title: Resolve the requested PR head before checking out manual reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event has no pull_request.head.sha, so this checks out github.ref, the branch selected when starting the workflow. The required pr_number can identify a PR on a different branch. In that case installation and the self-review tool run from the selected branch rather than the PR head; the previous workflow resolved headRefOid from the requested PR.

findings.title: Resolve the requested PR refs for manual reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event has no pull_request payload, so checkout falls back to github.ref, the branch selected when dispatching the workflow. If that branch differs from the requested PR head, the install and review steps run that branch’s code while targeting the supplied PR number. The same event also leaves PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA empty, whereas the previous workflow resolved both from the requested PR.

findings.title: Restore the larger Git output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit maxBuffer, spawnSync uses Node's 1 MiB default instead of the previous 64 MiB limit. A git diff exceeding that limit causes spawnSync to terminate the process and the helper to throw, so runLocal cannot review changes that previously worked. The error message may also omit the actual ENOBUFS cause because it only reports stderr.

findings.title: Restore the larger Git output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer reduces spawnSync's output limit from 64 MiB to Node's default of 1 MiB. A diff larger than 1 MiB causes Git to be terminated and the helper to throw, so runLocal cannot review changes that previously fit within the configured limit.

findings.title: Restore the larger buffer for Git output
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer lowers the spawnSync output limit from 64 MiB to Node's 1 MiB default. When a patch exceeds 1 MiB, git diff is terminated and runLocal throws before starting the review, even though patches up to 64 MiB previously worked.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews from satisfying required checks
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub treats a neutral check conclusion as successful for required-check branch protection. If review() or review posting throws, the Needlefish check now permits merging even though no review passed. Setting the process exit code to 1 does not change this separately posted check run.

findings.title: Select the target repository when fetching the PR diff
findings.whyItBreaks: The metadata request selects GITHUB_REPOSITORY explicitly, but gh pr diff resolves its repository from the process working directory. ghText does not use the supplied cwd. When the process runs outside that checkout, the command can fail or fetch a same-numbered PR from another repository, whose diff is then reviewed and posted against the target PR.

findings.title: Bind the reviewed checkout to the reported head commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The API returns the PR's current head, while changedFileSet and repository inspection still use the checkout's HEAD. If a new commit is pushed before an older Actions run fetches PR metadata, that run can review an older checkout yet post its result and check against the newer commit. Findings and policy inspection can therefore be based on stale files while the newer commit receives a passing check.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews from satisfying the required check
findings.whyItBreaks: When review or publication throws, the Needlefish check now completes with a neutral conclusion. GitHub accepts neutral required checks, so a PR can satisfy the Needlefish branch-protection requirement even though no review passed. Setting the process exit code to 1 does not change the conclusion of the separately posted Needlefish check.

findings.title: Fetch the diff from the configured repository
findings.whyItBreaks: Unlike the preceding API request, gh pr diff does not receive GITHUB_REPOSITORY, and ghText does not run in the supplied cwd. GitHub CLI therefore resolves the repository from the process working directory. If the adapter is invoked from outside the checkout, the command can fail or fetch the same PR number from another repository, while the result is posted to the configured repository.

findings.title: Bind the reviewed checkout and diff to the posted head SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The head SHA is taken from the live PR, while changedFileSet and the review workspace still use the checked-out HEAD, and the diff is fetched in a separate live request. If a new commit is pushed after an Actions run checks out an older commit, the run can review files from the old checkout yet post its review and check against the new commit. A push between the two GitHub requests can also make the diff and reported SHA disagree.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews blocking the required check
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub accepts a neutral check conclusion for a required status check. If review() or posting the review throws, the Needlefish check now reports neutral, so a PR can satisfy that required check even though the review failed. Setting process.exitCode affects the Actions job but does not make the separately posted Needlefish check fail.

findings.title: Select the repository explicitly when fetching the PR diff
findings.whyItBreaks: The metadata request selects GITHUB_REPOSITORY explicitly, but gh pr diff resolves the repository from the spawned process's working directory, not the cwd argument. When runGithub is called for a checkout other than the process working directory, the command can fail or fetch the same-numbered PR from another repository, while the resulting review is posted to GITHUB_REPOSITORY.

findings.title: Derive changed paths from the same comparison as the patch
findings.whyItBreaks: The GitHub PR diff compares the PR head with the merge base, while changedFileSet compares the current base commit directly with local HEAD. If both branches independently make the same change to a file, that file appears in the PR diff but not in the direct comparison. Its surface classification is omitted and inlineComments drops findings for it because changedPaths does not contain the path.

findings.title: Review a consistent checkout and PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head SHA and patch are fetched from GitHub, but changedFileSet and the review's repoPath still use the existing local checkout. If a PR is updated after the Actions checkout, the review can inspect old source files while the patch and posted check target the new head. A push between the metadata and diff requests can also make the patch and posted SHA refer to different revisions.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow now executes src/cli.ts from the PR head while exposing a token with pull-request and checks write permissions on a self-hosted runner. A PR can change that file to forge its own review or use the token and runner environment. The manual workflow path also accepts a PR number without the same-repository restriction. The previous workflow ran the tool from a separate main-branch checkout.

findings.title: Install the reviewer from a checkout that contains it
findings.whyItBreaks: The head commit contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, lockfile, or src/cli.ts. Installing from the PR checkout therefore cannot install the reviewer, so this workflow cannot review the current PR. The previous install used the separate frankekn/needlefish checkout.

findings.title: Keep PR-controlled code off the privileged runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The install now runs against the PR head on a self-hosted runner. A PR can add a package manifest and install script that executes arbitrary code there. The manual dispatch path accepts a PR number without the same-repository restriction applied to pull_request events, so a maintainer dispatching review of a fork PR can execute fork-controlled code. If installation succeeds, the PR-controlled CLI also receives a token with pull-request and checks write permissions.

A PR can modify src/cli.ts to post a favorable review or check, exfiltrate the token, or execute commands on the self-hosted runner. Reviews of this head therefore cannot install or start the reviewer. Previously those files came from the separate frankekn/needlefish checkout.

findings.title: Preserve severity normalization and the conservative fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation trimmed and uppercased severity before checking it, so a raw severity such as " p0 " produced P0. It now fails the exact membership check and becomes P3. Missing or invalid severities also change from P1 to P3. Because normalizeReview accepts unvalidated raw findings and returns these values to callers, serious findings can be presented as low priority, indistinguishable from genuine P3 findings.

findings.title: Preserve severity normalization before applying the fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: A review finding with severity " p0 " or "p0" previously normalized to P0. The new exact membership check rejects it and returns P3, so normalizeReview exposes a critical finding as low severity. Missing or otherwise invalid severities also now default to P3 instead of P1.

findings.title: Preserve severity normalization and a conservative fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: The public normalizer now converts values such as "p0" or " P1 " to P3, whereas it previously trimmed and uppercased them. Missing or otherwise invalid severities also now become P3 instead of P1. Callers cannot distinguish these failures from a genuine low-priority finding, so serious review findings can be reported at the lowest severity.

findings.title: Remove GitHub credentials from the Codex subprocess environment
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting the env option causes spawnSync to inherit process.env, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. Codex can read those values through its shell even in read-only mode, so malicious instructions in reviewed content can cause credentials to appear in the returned review output. The previous code explicitly removed these variables before spawning Codex.

findings.title: Remove GitHub tokens from the Codex subprocess environment
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env option, spawnSync passes process.env to Codex, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. A prompt or instruction in a repository being reviewed can cause the subprocess to read and disclose those credentials. The read-only filesystem sandbox does not prevent a token from appearing in command output or the model's response.

findings.title: Remove GitHub tokens from the Codex child environment
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting the env option makes spawnSync inherit the parent environment, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. The Codex process and commands it runs can now read those credentials while inspecting potentially untrusted repository content. A prompt injection in reviewed content could cause a token to be included in the review output; the read-only filesystem sandbox does not prevent environment-variable disclosure.

findings.title: Keep fork code off the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the same-repository guard allows the job to run for fork pull requests once GitHub permits the workflow to start. The job checks out the fork's head and runs both its dependency installation and its src/cli.ts on a self-hosted machine. A fork author can therefore execute arbitrary code with the runner's local privileges and access its persistent files, credentials, and network. GitHub's fork approval settings can limit when the job starts but do not make that code safe once it runs.

findings.title: Keep fork pull requests off the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the repository check allows a fork PR to reach this job. The job checks out the PR head and runs its dependency installation and src/cli.ts on a self-hosted machine, so a contributor can execute arbitrary code with the runner's filesystem and network access. Fork workflow approval, where enabled, does not make the checked-out code trusted.

findings.title: Restore the fork restriction on the self-hosted review job
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the job condition allows a forked pull request to reach the self-hosted runner. The job checks out the pull request's head and executes its dependency installation and src/cli.ts, so an attacker can run arbitrary code with access to the runner's local files, credentials, and network. Fork workflow approval settings may affect when the job starts but do not make execution safe once approved.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner timeout settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, setting NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 scheduled SIGKILL without a grace period; it now waits 5000 ms. Likewise, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now waits 2000 ms before returning when an escaped descendant keeps the pipes open. Existing configurations that use zero to minimize timeout cleanup will therefore wait seconds longer.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner timeout settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing configurations can set NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 to request immediate escalation after SIGTERM. This change substitutes the 5000 ms default, so a process that ignores SIGTERM continues running for five extra seconds. Likewise, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now waits 2000 ms before returning when an escaped descendant keeps the pipes open. Both values were accepted before this change.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration runner settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Zero was previously accepted for both runner duration environment variables. With NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0, a process that ignores SIGTERM now runs for another five seconds before SIGKILL. With NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0, an escaped descendant holding a pipe open now delays the timeout result by another two seconds. Both settings silently fall back to defaults after upgrade.

findings.title: Restore coverage for files outside selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first six risk-sorted hotspots are deep-reviewed. If the mapper returns more than six hotspots, or omits a changed file, files outside the selected hotspots receive no deep review and the final result does not disclose the missing coverage. The removed backstop previously placed those files in a tail hotspot.

findings.title: Preserve blocking risks returned by deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep review can return a blocking residual risk when it cannot verify a material path. The merge now discards every deep review's residual_risks and supplies an empty array to the critic, so the critic and verdict calculation cannot account for those known gaps. A large review can consequently report a passing verdict despite an explicitly blocked deep review.

findings.title: Keep distinct findings with matching titles
findings.whyItBreaks: The deduplication key no longer includes whyItBreaks. Two findings at the same file and starting line with the same category and normalized title but different failure paths now collapse to one; at equal severity the first wins. The removed finding never reaches the critic or final result, even when it describes a separate defect.

findings.title: Restore coverage for files outside selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review path selects at most six hotspots and now invokes deep review only for those hotspots. If the mapper returns a seventh hotspot with unique changed files, or omits a changed file from its hotspots, those files receive no deep review. The removed tail hotspot previously covered them, so the final result can miss defects in changed files.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from each deep review
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep review can return a blocking residual risk when it cannot verify part of a hotspot. The loop no longer collects those risks, and the merged candidate always supplies an empty list to the critic. Consequently the critic and final verdict cannot account for that reported uncertainty and may approve an incomplete review.

findings.title: Restore coverage for files outside selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: The deep-review loop now processes only the six selected hotspots. If the map pass omits a changed file or assigns it only to a seventh hotspot, that file receives no deep review and no residual risk is recorded. The critic receives only the patch stat for a large review, so the resulting review can miss a defect in that file.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from each deep review
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep result can contain residual_risks, including a blocking indication that evidence was insufficient. The merge now replaces all of them with an empty array before invoking the critic, so neither the critic nor the final verdict receives those warnings. A review with an unresolved blocking risk can consequently be reported as complete.

findings.title: Keep distinct findings that share a title and location
findings.whyItBreaks: Two findings in the same file, line, and category with the same normalized title now have the same key even when their explanations describe different defects. For example, two validation defects titled "Validate input" on the same line collapse into one, so the critic and final review never see the other defect.

findings.title: Preserve the requested focus in large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: For a patch over 30,000 characters or with more than 10 changed files, reviewLarge no longer sends bundle.focus to either the map pass or the deep passes. A review requested with a specific focus therefore proceeds without that instruction; the deep prompt also retains its {{FOCUS}} placeholder if the template contains it.

findings.title: Restore the requested focus in large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: For a patch over 30,000 characters or 10 changed files, reviewLarge no longer includes bundle.focus in the map input or substitutes it into the deep-review prompt. A caller requesting a focus therefore gets a large review whose map and hotspot reviewers never receive that request; small reviews still receive the full bundle.

findings.title: Preserve the requested focus in large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: For a patch over 30,000 characters or with more than 10 changed files, reviewLarge no longer passes bundle.focus to either the map pass or the per-hotspot deep passes. A caller requesting a focused review therefore gets an unfocused review, and the deep prompt can retain the literal {{FOCUS}} placeholder. Small reviews still receive the full bundle.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the minute count
findings.whyItBreaks: For a duration of 119,500 ms, the formatter now returns `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`. Durations from 59,500 through 59,999 ms similarly render as `60s` instead of `1m 0s`. This affects both per-call and total durations in the review output.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger now returns 0 for "0" and for strings such as "" that Number converts to zero. Its exported name and error message promise a positive integer, so callers can receive a value that violates the parser's contract.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function promises a positive integer, but parsePositiveInteger("0", label) now returns 0 instead of throwing. Number("") also produces 0, so empty input is accepted. Callers cannot rely on the parser to enforce its stated constraint.

findings.title: Reject zero when parsing a positive integer
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function promises a positive integer, but the new comparison accepts 0. It also accepts an empty or whitespace-only string because Number converts those inputs to 0. Callers relying on the parser's contract can therefore receive a non-positive value instead of an error.
